title: Nasal Cauterization — Chemical and Electrical
desc: In-office cauterization for epistaxis using silver nitrate or electrocautery to ablate the bleeding vessel.

blocks.content: Cauterization is used primarily for epistaxis — to ablate the bleeding vessel. Local anesthetic used is typically 1% or 2% lidocaine with epinephrine 1:100,000 — the epinephrine provides vasoconstriction that reduces active bleeding and improves visualization of the vessel.
Apply topical anesthetic — lidocaine or tetracaine to the nasal mucosa; allow adequate dwell time
Apply the silver nitrate tip directly to the vessel, rolling gently for a few seconds until a gray-white eschar forms — do not press hard or hold too long
Cut a small piece of Surgicel (approximately 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm), coat with mupirocin ointment, and apply over the cauterized area
Do not cauterize both sides of the septum in the same session — bilateral ischemia risks perforation
Post-procedure: no nose blowing 24–48 hours, no nose picking, nasal gel spray, no strenuous activity, no massage or chiropractic manipulation

Used when chemical cauterization has failed, the vessel is too large for silver nitrate, or the bleed is posterior and beyond Little's area. A bipolar or monopolar electrocautery unit is used under endoscopic visualization — in-office under local anesthesia or in the OR under general for posterior or arterial-level bleeds.

Posterior bleeds involve the sphenopalatine artery territory and may ultimately require OR-level electrocautery, endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation, or interventional radiology embolization in severe or recurrent cases.
For monopolar cautery: the grounding pad is placed on the patient's back or thigh. Know where the unit is, confirm it powers on, and have it set up before the provider enters the room.
